title: Spotted Dick
subtitle: Steamed suet pudding with currants and lemon
excerpt: A steamed suet pudding studded with currants and flavoured with lemon zest, served warm with custard or cream. One of the best-known British puddings, light despite its ingredients.
sourceNotes: Alexis Soyer, The Modern Housewife (1849), boiled suet puddings with dried fruit as a category. Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. Spotted dick by name first appears in British cookbooks in the 1840s. The 'spotted' refers to the currants; the etymology of 'dick' is debated but likely derives from 'dough' or 'diced'.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooled steamed pudding wrapped tightly for up to 3 months. Steam from frozen for 45 minutes or microwave in short bursts.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 3 days ahead and reheat by steaming for 30 minutes or microwaving, covered, for 3 minutes.

glossaryTerms.definition: The hard fat found around the kidneys and loins of beef or mutton. When used in puddings, it melts during steaming and creates a light, tender crumb with a characteristic richness. Vegetable suet is a plant-based alternative that works in the same way.

content.text: pudding packed with currants and flavoured with lemon zest. It is considerably lighter than its reputation suggests: the steam gives it a tender, almost sponge-like crumb. It should be served warm, as the fat in the suet sets to a greasy texture when the pudding cools.

Put {{self-raising-flour}} of self-raising flour and {{suet-shredded}} of suet in a large bowl. Add {{caster-sugar}} of caster sugar, {{currants}} of currants, the zest of {{lemon}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt. Mix together.
Add {{whole-milk}} of milk gradually and mix to a soft but not sticky dough. Shape into a log roughly 20 cm long and 8 cm wide.
Wrap the log loosely in buttered baking paper, then in foil, leaving room for expansion. Secure the ends firmly like a Christmas cracker.

Bring a large saucepan of water to the boil. Lower the pudding in, making sure the water comes halfway up the sides. Cover tightly and steam for 90 minutes, topping up the water with boiling water as needed.
Lift out and rest for 5 minutes. Unwrap and slice thickly. Serve warm with custard or double cream.

rows.cause: Too much milk used or dough overworked
rows.fix: The dough should be soft and just hold its shape. Add milk gradually and stop as soon as it comes together.

rows.cause: Served cold or at room temperature instead of warm
rows.fix: Spotted dick must be served warm. The suet becomes unpleasant as it cools and firms. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

rows.cause: Dough too loose, or currants too heavy relative to the mixture
rows.fix: Toss the currants in a little flour before adding them to the mix. This helps them suspend in the dough.

rows.symptom: Foil splits and water gets in
rows.cause: Not wrapped tightly enough or too much water in the pan
rows.fix: Wrap in two layers of foil and pleat the top rather than twisting it. Keep the water at a steady steam, not a violent boil.

content.text: Spotted dick has been on British menus since at least the 1840s. The suet pudding tradition it belongs to is specifically British: steaming in a pudding basin or cloth was the standard baking method when ovens were expensive or unreliable. By the twentieth century, spotted dick was associated primarily with school dinners and works canteens. It appears in tinned form as a Heinz product, sold globally, and this version has made the name familiar far beyond Britain.
